You read the column? Half my colleagues wrote to complain about it, and not one of them had read past the second paragraph.
I read it twice. What struck me was the honesty about the memoirs — the old version did not hold up to scrutiny and everybody had been quoting it for years.
That is the part they object to. Nobody minds a new document. What they mind is being told that the old story was received wisdom rather than research.
Which it usually is, at that distance. Although I would not go so far as to say the whole account was wrong — only that the tidiness was overstated.
No sooner do you say that in a seminar than somebody accuses you of relativism. As if admitting a version is provisional meant admitting it is worthless.
In medicine we live with that permanently. The guidance changes and people hear it as an admission that the earlier guidance was a lie.
Exactly the same argument, different building. So what would change your mind about the current reading?
A document that casts doubt on the timeline. Not an opinion — a date that does not fit.
Not only does it use new documents, but it also admits what it cannot explain.

What has been overstated is the tidiness of it.
In thirty years this will look like a product of its time.

So, the archive. Four hundred and twelve boxes, opened over nineteen months, and most of it is exactly what you would expect: budgets, staffing, complaints about the heating. But three documents changed the shape of the thing. The most important is a memorandum from 1979, ten years before the events we are discussing, in which two departments are already arguing about precisely the question that would later be presented as sudden. Ten years. Now, why did the old account survive so long? Not because anybody was hiding anything. It survived because it was elegant, and because nobody had a particular reason to test it. That is usually the answer, and it is far less interesting than a conspiracy.

I want to be fair to this book, because the research is serious and nobody disputes the archive work. My objection is narrower than my colleagues' and, I think, harder to answer. The author treats one memorandum as decisive. Three other documents from the same eighteen months point the other way, and they are dealt with in a single footnote. Now, I am not accusing him of dishonesty. Nothing of the kind. I think he is simply too fond of his own finding, which is the most human failing there is in this profession. Read the book. Then read the footnote, and ask yourself why it is a footnote.
